abstract: Chronic inflammatory injury promotes epithelial metaplasia, and progression from metaplasia to dysplasia is a recognized initiating event in carcinogenesis, as metaplastic cells exhibit heightened susceptibility to genetic alterations. In the pancreas, persistent acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) can progress to pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), yet the mechanisms that determine whether ADM resolves or persists with fibrosis and sustained inflammation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify CD73 as a central regulator of ADM fate, tissue repair, and immune microenvironment remodeling during chronic pancreatic injury. Analysis of previously published single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from chronic pancreatitis (CP) tissues identified enrichment of Nt5e, which encodes CD73, within Hnf1{beta} ADM populations. Hnf1bCreERT2 and CD73fl/fl;Hnf1bCreERT2 mice were treated with caerulein for 4 weeks to induce pancreatitis and ADM prior to tamoxifen-induced deletion of CD73 in HNF1B-expressing metaplastic epithelial cells. Histologic phenotyping and immune profiling were performed using immunohistochemistry and imaging mass cytometry. Metaplasia-specific CD73 deletion exacerbated pancreatic injury and fibrosis, impaired epithelial proliferation and recovery of the acinar compartment, and altered the abundance and spatial organization of inflammatory cells. Ex vivo ADM assays further demonstrated that CD73 loss increased ADM formation and the production of MCP-1 and TIMP-1. These findings identify CD73 as a context-dependent checkpoint linking epithelial plasticity and immune modulation during chronic pancreatic injury and tissue repair.
